title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
description:
# Kth Largest Element in an Array

Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the kth largest element in sorted order.

Count duplicate occurrences separately. For example, `[3,3,2]` sorted from largest to smallest is still `[3,3,2]`, so its second largest value is `3`.

## Example

Input: `nums = [3,2,1,5,6,4], k = 2`

Output: `5`

## Constraints

`1 <= k <= nums.length <= 10^5`. Values may be negative, repeated many times, already sorted, reverse sorted, or near the stated value boundary `-10^4 <= nums[i] <= 10^4`.
initialCode: class Solution { public int findKthLargest(int[] nums, int k) { return 0; } }

solutions.name: Min Heap of Size k
solutions.description:
## Approach

Maintain a min heap containing the largest `k` values seen so far. Push each number into the heap; when the heap grows beyond `k`, remove the smallest kept value. After every number has been processed, the heap root is the kth largest value.

## Key Insight

The heap stores the current top-k multiset, not the top-k distinct values. Its smallest value is exactly the boundary element that would be at position `k` in descending order.

## Complexity Analysis

Each of the `n` values performs a heap operation on a heap of size at most `k`, so the time complexity is `O(n log k)`. The heap stores `O(k)` values.

solutions.name: Quickselect Partition
solutions.description:
## Approach

Convert kth largest into index `nums.length - k` in ascending order. Partition the array around a pivot until that target index is placed in its final sorted position, then return the value at that index.

## Key Insight

Selection needs only the target position, not a fully sorted array. Partitioning discards the side that cannot contain the target after each step, which is why quickselect is the standard expected-linear route.

## Complexity Analysis

Randomized pivots give expected `O(n)` time, while consistently unlucky pivots can degrade to `O(n^2)`. The partitioning is in-place, so auxiliary space is `O(1)`.

solutions.name: Counting Buckets by Value Range
solutions.description:
## Approach

Use the value bounds to count how many times each integer appears. Scan counts from the largest value down, subtracting frequencies from `k` until the kth position lands inside one bucket.

## Key Insight

Because the value range is small and fixed, positions in descending sorted order can be recovered from frequencies without comparing or moving individual elements.

## Complexity Analysis

Let `R` be the value range size. Counting costs `O(n)`, scanning the buckets costs `O(R)`, and the count array stores `O(R)` integers.

solutions.name: Full Sort Baseline
solutions.description:
## Approach

Sort the whole array in ascending order and return `nums[nums.length - k]`. This is the simplest way to verify the meaning of kth largest and duplicate counting.

## Key Insight

After ascending sort, the largest element is at index `n - 1`, so the kth largest is exactly `n - k`. This baseline is slower than selection but is a useful correctness anchor.

## Complexity Analysis

Sorting costs `O(n log n)` time. Java's primitive array sort is in-place aside from recursion/implementation stack space, commonly described as `O(log n)` auxiliary space.
